title: The history of the northern lights
tagline: From a 'five-coloured light' in ancient China and elders' stories in Alaska to spacecraft that fly through the Sun's atmosphere.
intro: People have looked up at the aurora for thousands of years. Early writers recorded it as an omen or a story. Over the 1700s and 1800s, observers tied it to compass needles, to the Sun and to the colour of single atoms. In the 1900s, satellites showed that the lights are powered by the solar wind and Earth's magnetic field. Some details are still argued over, and this history says so where they are.

eras.name: Old records and old stories
eras.summary: Chroniclers in China, Assyria, Babylon, Greece and Japan write down strange lights in the sky. Peoples of the Arctic and Australia tell their own stories about them. Nobody yet knows what causes them.

eras.name: A link to magnetism
eras.summary: Observers notice that compass needles twitch when the lights shine. A great storm in 1859 shows a link to the Sun. Birkeland and Størmer try to explain the lights with experiments, mathematics and photographs.

eras.name: What makes the colours
eras.summary: Spectrographs find a green line in the aurora. A laboratory copies it in 1925, and later work traces it to oxygen. Rockets catch the electrons that make the glow.

eras.name: The space age
eras.summary: Theory and spacecraft reveal the solar wind, the magnetosphere, the radiation belts and magnetic reconnection. The pieces of the aurora puzzle fall into place.

eras.name: Storms and probes
eras.summary: A storm blacks out a power grid in 1989. A probe flies through the Sun's atmosphere in 2021. A superstorm in 2024 pushes the lights to low latitudes.

events.title: Elders in Alaska tell what the lights are
events.who: Iñupiaq and Athabascan elders and storytellers
events.text: In Iñupiaq cultures of northern Alaska, the northern lights are the spirits of ancestors playing kickball in the sky. The Iñupiaq word is kiuġuyat or kiuġiyaq. In many Athabascan cultures, elders say caribou can be found beneath the lights, and that red lights are a sign of bloodshed or war. The University of Alaska notes that these stories vary by culture, community and person.
events.why: Elders also describe the lights as a source of light, a way to navigate and a sign of coming weather, which is knowledge as well as story.

events.title: Aboriginal Australian stories of the southern lights
events.text: Wikipedia reports that in Aboriginal Australian traditions the aurora australis is commonly linked with fire. It says the Gunditjmara people called auroras puae buae, meaning ashes, and the Gunai people saw them as bushfires in the spirit world.
events.why: The lights shine over both poles, and people in the south have their own stories about them.

events.title: A five-coloured light in the Bamboo Annals
events.who: Chinese chroniclers; identified by Marinus van der Sluijs and Hisashi Hayakawa (2022)
events.text: The Bamboo Annals mention a five-coloured light in the northern sky near the end of King Zhao's reign. Researchers favour 977 or 957 BCE, depending on how the reign is dated. They call it the oldest datable candidate aurora, not a certain one.
events.why: It shows that a big storm once lit the sky far from the poles, and records like this help scientists track the Sun over thousands of years.

events.title: Assyrian scribes note strange lights
events.text: Cuneiform tablets dated 679–655 BCE record candidate auroras. Before the Bamboo Annals entry was identified, these were the oldest known candidates.
events.why: They are early evidence that people kept careful written records of the night sky.

events.title: A Babylonian diary, under Nebuchadnezzar II
events.text: A Babylonian astronomical diary entry from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II, dated 567 BCE, is listed as an early candidate aurora. Some scientists have linked Ezekiel's vision of 594 or 593 BCE to aurora too, but that link is thought less reliable.
events.why: Babylon's daily sky diaries are one of the best long records of the heavens.

events.title: Aristotle describes 'chasms' and 'trenches' in the sky
events.text: In Meteorology, Book I, Aristotle writes of sky appearances such as 'chasms', 'trenches' and blood-red colours. He says they share a cause with shooting stars and flames, and that the air takes on different colours. Astronomy magazine says he described the aurora.
events.why: It is an early attempt to explain the lights with natural causes, not with gods.

events.title: A red sign like a pheasant's tail over Japan
events.who: Nihon Shoki; studied by Ryuho Kataoka and colleagues
events.text: The Nihon Shoki records a red sign in the sky on 30 December 620 CE, shaped like a pheasant's tail and more than 10 degrees long. Older readings took it for a comet. A 2020 study argues that a fan-shaped red aurora over Japan fits the description. It is an interpretation, not proof.
events.why: Red aurora can reach mid-latitudes in strong storms, so old records from Japan and China help us study past space weather.

events.title: A name for the lights
events.text: A NASA timeline says Galileo may have introduced the term 'aurora borealis' in 1619, a view it credits to the historian George Siscoe. Astronomy magazine says he coined it. Older books credit Pierre Gassendi instead.
events.why: The name means 'northern dawn' and it is still the name we use.

events.title: Gassendi describes a great display over France
events.text: A great aurora was seen across France in September 1621. Gassendi wrote about it, and an old edition of the Britannica says he named it aurora borealis. Wikipedia says the term first appears in his 1649 account. After this, no display was recorded in Europe for more than 80 years, according to Halley.
events.why: The lights were then rare in Europe for decades, which makes the next big display a landmark.

events.title: Halley writes a history of the lights
events.text: A bright aurora in 1716 drew wide attention in Europe. Halley published a history of the phenomenon in Philosophical Transactions, No. 347. He reported that no such display had been recorded for more than 80 years, and none of any size since 1574.
events.why: It was one of the first attempts to treat the aurora as a natural event to be recorded and explained.

events.title: Compass needles twitch when the lights shine
events.text: Hiorter, Celsius's assistant, made observations from 1740–41 showing that the compass needle moved at the same time as auroral outbreaks. He published the result in 1747 and said Celsius had noticed it first. Uppsala University says they found that bigger needle swings matched stronger aurora.
events.why: It was the first sign that the aurora is linked to Earth's magnetic field.

events.title: The Carrington storm
events.text: On 1 September 1859, Carrington saw a flash of white light near sunspots at about 11 in the morning. About 17 hours later the night sky lit up over North America, as far south as Panama. Surges hit the telegraph network and magnetic instruments went off scale. Estimates of its size differ a lot, from about -850 to -1,760 nT on the Dst index.
events.why: It was the first clear sign that a storm on the Sun can disturb Earth.

events.title: Ångström finds the green line
events.text: In 1868 Ångström used a theodolite fitted with a transmission grating and found the aurora's green line at about 5578 Å. JSTOR Daily, citing the historian Helge Kragh, gives 1869. The green did not match any known element, so some scientists proposed an unknown auroral gas.
events.why: The light of the aurora had a fingerprint, and it was a puzzle for the next 55 years.

events.title: Birkeland builds a little Earth
events.text: From about 1895 Birkeland tried to explain in the lab why aurora appears near the poles. Around 1900 he put a small magnetised sphere, a terrella or 'little Earth', in a glass tank and fired electrons at it. The beam bent toward the poles. In 1913 he built a much larger version.
events.why: It showed how a magnet can steer charged particles toward its poles, the idea behind the funnel in this box.

events.title: Størmer photographs the aurora from two places
events.text: Størmer took his first aurora photographs in 1909. Stations at least 5 km apart, linked by telephone, photographed the same aurora at the same moment. By triangulation the average height came out as just over 100 km, with a lowest measurement of 71 km. Wikipedia says more than 12,000 auroras were triangulated from 1911.
events.why: The lights were shown to be in the upper atmosphere, not in the clouds.

events.title: The green line is made in a laboratory
events.text: The green line could not be reproduced in a laboratory until 1924. McLennan and Shrum reported their result in 1925. Shrum produced the line using helium-oxygen mixtures. Later work traced it to oxygen alone. Kragh says McLennan, the professor, got most of the credit.
events.why: It finally tied the aurora's green to oxygen atoms, which is the glow chapter of this box.

events.title: Chapman and Ferraro: a cavity around the Earth
events.text: Chapman and Ferraro proposed that the Sun sends out clouds of plasma. Earth's magnetic field holds a cloud off and carves a cavity that holds Earth inside. NASA calls the idea prophetic, with one fix: the plasma flows from the Sun all the time as the solar wind.
events.why: It is the first picture of the magnetic shield that guards the Earth.

events.title: Comet tails point to a stream from the Sun
events.text: Biermann saw that dust tails fit the push of sunlight, but ion tails were accelerated far too hard. He argued that a 'solar corpuscular radiation' must be pushing them.
events.why: It was the first strong hint of a steady flow from the Sun.

events.title: A rocket flies into the aurora
events.who: Meredith, Gottlieb and James Van Allen; Carl McIlwain
events.text: In 1954 detectors on a rocket launched into an aurora gave the first direct look at auroral electrons. In 1959 McIlwain used a rocket to identify the particles as electrons with an average energy equal to acceleration through 6,000 volts. NOAA now describes aurora as electrons hitting oxygen and nitrogen 80 to 500 km above the ground.
events.why: It proved the lights are made by streams of electrons.

events.title: Explorer 1 finds the radiation belts
events.text: Explorer 1 carried Van Allen's Geiger counter into orbit on 31 January 1958. Its readings were puzzling and at times fell to zero. A student, Carl McIlwain, suggested the counter was overloaded by intense radiation. Explorer 3 (26 March 1958) supported this. Van Allen announced the belts in May 1958. Later flights found a second, outer belt.
events.why: Earth's magnetic field traps charged particles in belts, which is how the shield works.

events.title: Parker predicts the solar wind
events.text: In a 1958 paper in the Astrophysical Journal, Parker predicted a solar wind and the spiral shape of the Sun's magnetic field. The reviewers were doubtful, and one called it utter nonsense. The editor, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, could not find an error and published it.
events.why: It explained how the Sun sends particles and magnetic fields all the way to Earth.

events.title: Dungey: the field lines can reconnect
events.text: Dungey's short paper 'Interplanetary Magnetic Field and the Auroral Zones' was published on 15 January 1961. It proposed that Earth's magnetic field lines can link up with the Sun's, in what is now called the Dungey cycle. Later work found that the dayside and night-side steps do not match as closely as he first assumed.
events.why: It explained how the solar wind's energy gets in and is funnelled to the poles.

events.title: Explorer 12 sees the edge of the shield
events.text: NASA says the magnetopause, the boundary of Earth's magnetic cavity, was first observed in 1961 by Explorer 12.
events.why: The shield became something that could be measured, not just imagined.

events.title: Akasofu describes the auroral substorm
events.text: Shortly after earning his doctorate in 1961, Akasofu, a Japanese researcher, discovered and described the auroral substorm. It explained why the aurora can be quiet for long stretches and then burst into about an hour of intense activity.
events.why: It gave a name and a shape to the sudden brightening and dancing of the lights.

events.title: Mariner 2 measures the solar wind
events.text: Mariner 2's plasma detector revealed the solar wind as a continuous stream blowing off the Sun. Physics Today says Luna 1 had detected solar-wind particles about a year earlier, and Mariner 2 confirmed it in 1962.
events.why: It turned Parker's theory into a measurement.

events.title: Alfvén wins the Nobel Prize in Physics
events.where: Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, Sweden
events.text: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences gave Alfvén the 1970 Nobel Prize in Physics for fundamental work and discoveries in magnetohydrodynamics, with fruitful applications in different parts of plasma physics.
events.why: Magnetohydrodynamics is the physics of magnetised, flowing plasma, which is what the solar wind and magnetosphere are.

events.title: Joan Feynman finds a flag for solar storms
events.text: Working at NASA Ames in the early 1970s, Joan Feynman found that helium in the solar wind rises sharply when flares accelerate solar particles. That enrichment is now used to identify coronal mass ejections.
events.why: Telling storms from the ordinary wind is a step toward forecasting the aurora.

events.title: A storm blacks out Quebec
events.text: At about 2:45 in the morning on 13 March 1989, currents driven through the ground tripped safety systems on the Hydro-Québec grid. Up to six million people lost power for as long as nine hours. Auroras were seen as far south as Texas and Cuba. The storm's Dst was -589 nT.
events.why: It showed that space weather can switch off a modern power grid.

events.title: THEMIS finds the trigger of a substorm
events.who: Vassilis Angelopoulos and the THEMIS team
events.text: Five THEMIS satellites launched in February 2007. On 26 February 2008 they watched a substorm start in space while ground cameras in Canada and Alaska saw the aurora brighten. The team reported in Science that magnetic reconnection about a third of the way to the Moon triggers the onset. NASA calls it the first confirmation.
events.why: It linked the sudden brightening of the lights to reconnection in Earth's tail.

events.title: Parker Solar Probe flies through the Sun's atmosphere
events.text: The probe, named for Eugene Parker, launched on 12 August 2018. On 28 April 2021, on its eighth flyby, it crossed the Alfvén critical surface, where the Sun's atmosphere ends and the solar wind begins. It spent a few hours inside the corona.
events.why: A spacecraft has now sampled the place where the solar wind is born.

events.title: A superstorm paints the sky at low latitudes
events.text: Five coronal mass ejections that left the Sun on 8–9 May drove the storm. Its Dst reached -412 nT, the sixth strongest since 1957 in that index, according to the authors. Naked-eye aurora was reported down to about 23° magnetic latitude in Namibia and about 24° in India. Values are provisional.
events.why: It was the strongest storm since 2003 and showed what a superstorm looks like in an age of satellites.

people.name: Kristian Birkeland
people.note: Built a 'little Earth' in a tank and showed an electron beam bending to its poles.

people.name: Carl Størmer
people.note: Measured the height of the aurora by triangulation.

people.name: Anders Celsius
people.note: Credited by Hiorter with first noticing the compass needle's reaction to the lights.

people.name: Olof Hiorter
people.note: Published the 1747 report on needle movements during auroras.

people.name: Anders Ångström
people.note: Found the aurora's green line with a grating spectrograph.

people.name: Gordon Shrum
people.note: Made the green line in the lab in 1925, working with John McLennan.

people.name: Eugene Parker
people.note: Predicted the solar wind in 1958 and had a NASA probe named for him.

people.name: James Dungey
people.note: Proposed in 1961 that Earth's field lines reconnect with the Sun's.

people.name: Joan Feynman
people.note: Found that helium rises in the solar wind during flares; her aurora work stressed a southward field.

people.name: Syun-Ichi Akasofu
people.note: Described the auroral substorm and later led the Geophysical Institute in Alaska.

people.name: Ryuho Kataoka
people.note: Led the 2020 study of the 620 CE 'pheasant tail' record.

people.name: Fannie Akpik
people.note: Speaks in the film Kiuġuyat about the Iñupiat lunar calendar and its names for the Sun's position and light.

series.title: How strong the great storms were
series.unit: nT (size of the drop in the Dst index)
series.caption: The bigger the number, the stronger the storm. The 1859 value is an estimate that scientists disagree on, and Dst values from different eras are not strictly comparable.

points.label: Carrington, 1859: about 1,760 (Tsurutani et al.); Siscoe et al. give about 850
March 1989 (Quebec): Dst -589; the faster SYM-H index reached -710

facts: NOAA says the aurora typically forms 80 to 500 km above the Earth's surface.
Explorer 1's Geiger counter sometimes read zero because the radiation was so strong it overloaded the counter.
In March 1989 the Hydro-Québec grid went offline in under 90 seconds, according to Wikipedia.
Størmer's photographs put the average aurora just over 100 km up.
In May 2024 the lights were seen with the naked eye in Namibia and India.
